beats.headline: Why does your Java app take 10 seconds to boot?
beats.subline: HotSpot JVM is built for long-running servers, but serverless environments demand instant startup.
beats.narration: HotSpot JVM is a beast for long-running servers, but in serverless environments, its JIT warmup and memory footprint are massive liabilities. Let's look at the modern alternatives.

beats.title: JIT vs AOT Compilation

nodes.label: HotSpot
nodes.detail: JIT compiles at runtime; high peak throughput.

nodes.label: GraalVM
nodes.detail: AOT compiles to native binary; instant startup.

beats.narration: HotSpot optimizes as it runs, which is great for throughput but slow for startup. GraalVM Native Image shifts that work to build-time, producing a standalone binary that boots in milliseconds.

beats.title: Reachability Metadata

steps.explanation: Native Image uses static analysis. Reflection breaks it.
You must explicitly tell the compiler what to keep.

beats.narration: Because Native Image uses a closed-world assumption, it strips unused code. If you use reflection, you need reachability metadata to keep those classes alive, or your app will crash.

beats.title: HotSpot vs GraalVM
beats.narration: Choose HotSpot for long-lived services where throughput is king. Choose GraalVM if you're building scale-to-zero functions where every millisecond of startup counts.

beats.title: Part 1 Locked In
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 2): Spring Boot 3, Quarkus, and Micronaut strategies →
beats.narration: That's the trade-off. Next, we compare how Spring Boot 3, Quarkus, and Micronaut handle the move to cloud-native.

beats.headline: Is Spring Boot 3 actually cloud-native?
beats.subline: It's not just about the framework; it's about how they handle build-time augmentation.
beats.narration: Spring Boot 3, Quarkus, and Micronaut all claim to be cloud-native, but they use wildly different strategies to move work from runtime to build-time.

beats.title: Spring AOT Hints

steps.explanation: Processes beans and conditions during build.

beats.narration: Spring Boot 3 uses an AOT build phase to inspect your context and generate plain Java code for bean wiring, bypassing the heavy runtime reflection.

beats.title: Framework Approaches
beats.narration: Quarkus uses build-time bytecode augmentation, while Micronaut relies on annotation processing to generate everything at compile-time. Both are built for native speed.

beats.title: Build-Time vs Runtime
beats.narration: By moving dependency injection and proxy generation to build-time, these frameworks eliminate the need for costly classpath scanning when your container starts.

beats.title: Part 2 Locked In
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 3): Solving cold starts with SnapStart and CRaC →
beats.narration: All three are solid, just pick your ecosystem. Next, we tackle the cold start problem in serverless using SnapStart and CRaC.

beats.headline: Stop the 5-second cold start.
beats.subline: AWS Lambda SnapStart and Project CRaC let you checkpoint your JVM state.
beats.narration: If your Lambda takes 5 seconds to boot, you're losing users. SnapStart and CRaC solve this by taking a snapshot of your initialized JVM and restoring it instantly.

beats.title: Checkpoint & Restore
beats.narration: SnapStart runs your init logic once, then snapshots the entire microVM. When a request arrives, it restores that snapshot, skipping the heavy classloading phase.

beats.title: CRaC Lifecycle Hooks
beats.narration: The danger? State. If you have open sockets or random seeds, they get cloned. Use CRaC hooks to clean up before the checkpoint and re-initialize after the restore.

beats.title: SnapStart vs Native
beats.narration: SnapStart keeps full JVM compatibility, while Native Image gives you the smallest possible footprint. Choose based on your memory constraints.

beats.title: Part 3 Locked In
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 4): Optimizing containers with Jib and jlink →
beats.narration: SnapStart is a game changer for Java on Lambda. Finally, we'll look at optimizing your container images to keep your deployments lean.

beats.headline: Stop shipping 500MB container images.
beats.subline: Jib, Buildpacks, and jlink can slash your image size and speed up CI.
beats.narration: Shipping a 500MB image for a simple service is wasteful. Let's optimize your container delivery with Jib, Buildpacks, and jlink.

beats.title: Jib Plugin
beats.narration: Jib builds OCI images without a Docker daemon. It layers your app perfectly, so changing one line of code only rebuilds the tiny classes layer, not the whole image.

beats.title: Custom Runtime with jlink
beats.narration: Use jlink to strip the JDK down to only the modules your app needs. It trims away man pages and headers, saving over 100MB per image.

beats.title: Optimization Tools
beats.narration: Jib wins on CI speed and ease of use, while jlink is the ultimate tool for shrinking your runtime footprint. Use them together for maximum impact.
